item.description:
Red Sea Film Festival cancelled as Israeli-US war on Iran hits Saudi Arabia

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 09/21/2026 - 15:34
Regional wars which now includes Yemen are increasingly disrupting Riyadh’s drive to become a global entertainment and tourism hub
Italian top model Alessandra Ambrosio poses on the red carpet of the awards ceremony of the 4th edition of Red Sea Film Festival in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on 12 December 2024 (Patrick Baz /Red Sea Film Festival/AFP)
Off

The Red Sea Film Festival has cancelled its sixth edition as the Israeli-US war on Iran and Saudi Arabia’s escalating conflict with the Houthis continue to disrupt the kingdom’s flagship international events.

The festival, the Arab world’s most prominent film event and market, had been scheduled to run in Jeddah from 3 to 12 December.

Organisers said it would instead return in the final quarter of 2027 with a “renewed vision and a program that continues to celebrate cinema and filmmakers from Saudi Arabia, the region and around the world,” according to a statement.

The festival did not directly cite the wars in announcing the cancellation, saying instead that logistical considerations had shaped the decision.

“The decision follows a comprehensive review of a range of considerations relating to the timing of the next edition, including the logistical requirements involved in staging an international event of this scale,” the statement said.

It added that the festival would return at “the right time and under the right conditions”.

It is the second major international event Saudi Arabia has lost this year as regional wars increasingly disrupt the kingdom’s efforts to promote itself as a global entertainment and tourism hub.

Formula One cancelled the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix, scheduled for 17-19 April at the Jeddah Corniche Circuit, amid the fallout from the Israeli-US war on Iran.

Saudi Arabia is also facing a sharp escalation in its conflict with the Houthis in neighbouring Yemen. The group has targeted Saudi cities, oil infrastructure and Red Sea oil shipments.

Saudi Arabia established the Red Sea Film Festival in 2019, with its first edition taking place after the kingdom ended its 35-year ban on commercial cinemas.

The festival and its Red Sea Souk market have since become central to Riyadh’s push to build an international film and television industry and reduce the economy’s dependence on oil.

Executives from Netflix, Amazon, Disney and regional broadcaster MBC have attended the market in Jeddah.

When the festival returns in 2027, it will also face renewed regional competition from the Dubai International Film Festival, which is due to return on 8 December.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Gulf states need 'good relations' with Iran as part of new security framework, Qatar's PM says
item.description:
Gulf states need 'good relations' with Iran as part of new security framework, Qatar's PM says

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 09/21/2026 - 15:09
Meanwhile, Qatar's energy minister says the US is 'wrong' to think the Strait of Hormuz can be made irrelevant, adding no plans for gas pipeline
Qatar's Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani attends a meeting in Manama on 25 June 2026 (Eric Lee/AFP)
Off

Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani has said the Middle East needs a new "regional security framework" that includes Iran, adding that the war against the Islamic Republic should be a "wake up call" for the region.

"Iran is our neighbour," Al Thani told the Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sunday.

"We have to act together responsibly as a region and to make sure that we are having good relations with Iran," he said.

"We are hoping this war is a wake-up call for everyone."

The Qatari prime minister's comments came hours after reports claimed the US was planning to restart direct attacks after months of reduced violence.

US President Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the State Department to all US citizens in the Middle East.

Trump also reportedly told a Fox News reporter "very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future" and that the options he was considering were "wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal".

Since the US and Israel went to war with Iran more than six months ago, Gulf Arab states have borne the brunt of Iran's reprisals despite some urging Washington to end the US-Israeli war.

The Islamic Republic has repeatedly attacked US military bases across the region, with photos seen by Middle East Eye showing widespread damage. The Trump administration has yet to acknowledge the extent of the damage sustained. 

The impact of the war on the global economy has also been highly damaging, particularly after Iran closed off the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway.

The number of vessels sailing through the strait has dwindled, with preliminary ship-tracking data from Kpler showing only 12 commodity vessels crossing over the weekend. 

'Few cards to play': Saudi Arabia faces limited options against Houthis with allies out
Read More »

Earlier on Sunday, Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE’s president, said at a separate event that the region needed a "new mindset," and called for negotiations to end the war to include an "Iranian-Arab" element.

For Qatar and its Gulf neighbours, the disruption is becoming an increasingly direct economic threat.

Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq and the UAE all depend heavily on the Strait of Hormuz for energy shipments and imports. Meanwhile, the crisis is also threatening Qatar's plans to expand its liquefied natural gas (LNG) production.

Earlier this month, Qatar extended its force majeure for LNG shipments to early November because of the maritime blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. 

But the vulnerability of any Strait of Hormuz bypass has been underscored in recent weeks with Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline disabled by a drone attack the kingdom said emanated from militias in Iraq.

The attack came amid a sweeping Houthi offensive in Yemen that put the group in control of the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline.

The Houthis have imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabian shipping. They attacked Riyadh airport over the weekend.

Qatar says 'no pipeline plans'

The East-West pipeline cuts through Saudi Arabia's hinterland and terminates at the port of Yanbu, allowing Saudi Arabia to export approximately two-thirds of its pre-war oil volumes, or around four million barrels per day (bpd).

But the kingdom cancelled oil loadings at Yanbu last week and informed refining customers in Europe that they will not receive crude allocations in October.

The UAE has been one of the more vocal states saying it plans to increase investments in pipelines to bypass Hormuz, but other oil producers, like Bahrain and Kuwait, have less options.

Qatari Energy Minister Saad al-Kaabi said the US was "wrong" that new investments in pipelines could make the Strait of Hormuz irrelevant in two years.

"I mean, maybe this is his view. I think this is completely wrong," Kaabi said on Sunday at the Qatar Economic Forum.

"We have decided not to do pipelines, and I think the decision in Qatar was based on commercial and technical [reasons], and we are only going to be using the straits," he added, ruling out any gas pipeline investments.

item.description:
Hegseth slammed for 'blasphemous' use of Bible passage in military recruitment drive

Hegseth led a chant in front of young military recruits that had the refrain 'send me to go fight the Islamists'
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth poses for a photo during a game at Kyle Field in College Station, Texas, on 19 September 2026 (Zach Del Bello/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has come under fire for a military “Send Me Tour” that draws on biblical verses and Christian scripture to recruit new soldiers. 

Hegseth visited Texas A&M University over the weekend as part of the tour, which is based on a well-known refrain from the Old Testament Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6, Verse 8, in which God asks, "Who shall I send?" and the prophet Isaiah replies, “Lord, I am here. Send me”.

Isaiah is a prophet for both Jews and Christians. Although the Quran does not explicitly mention him, some Islamic literature regards him as a prophet. 

Hegseth was filmed in front of a group of young college students, invoking Isaiah’s biblical language for a war chant.

“For 250 years of this country, there have been men and women who raised their right hand and said, ‘Send me,’” Hegseth shouted.

“Send me to go fight the Redcoats. Send me to go fight the Communists. Send me to go fight the Islamists,” he shouted.

Hegseth’s channelling of religious rhetoric drew sharp condemnation from many Christian religious groups in the US.

“This is not only a blatant violation of the 1st amendment, it is blasphemous and taking the Lord’s name in vain. He is using scripture to frame military service as a kind of Christian religious crusade,” Benjamin Cremer, a Methodist reverend, wrote.

“This is Christian extremism. If a radical Muslim military leader was doing this in another country, using the Quran to stoke commitment to a holy war among young recruits, the condemnation from American Christians would be swift and severe. The hypocrisy is astounding,” Cremer added.

Other observers on social media in the US reacted with fury to Hegseth instrumentalising a Bible passage to recruit US soldiers.

“Pete Hegseth twists Bible quote to justify US wars!” another commentator wrote on X.

“In the Book of Isaiah, the prophet’s cry of ‘Send me!’ was a request to be directed to preach repentance and divine judgement to the ancient Israelites. It wasn’t about going on a series of global killing sprees,” the commentator added.

Weaponising Christianity

This is not the first time Hegseth has drawn scrutiny for his attempt to instrumentalise Christianity for military purposes.

In April, he read a fake Bible verse from Quentin Tarantino's 1994 cult classic film, Pulp Fiction, during a Christian prayer and worship service at the Pentagon, which he holds regularly. 

US: Hegseth reads fake Bible verse from Pulp Fiction during Pentagon sermon
Read More »

Hegseth has also sparked outrage for framing military efforts, such as the war on Iran, as a religious imperative.

During one Pentagon prayer service, Hegseth called for "overwhelming violence of action against those who deserve no mercy."

"Let every round find its mark against the enemies of righteousness and our great nation," Hegseth said. 

The US and Israel launched a war on Iran in February. At the beginning of the conflict, US commanders from every branch of the military told their units that the war was “anointed by Jesus” and would bring about his return to Earth as part of "Armageddon", resulting in scores of complaints from military personnel.

The Military Religious Freedom Foundation, an organisation dedicated to ensuring that all members of the US military are guaranteed religious freedom, told Middle East Eye that it had received more than 200 similar complaints from personnel serving in the army, navy, air force, marine corps, and space force at the time.

Hegseth has emerged as one of the most vociferous advocates for the US war on Iran, often taking a combative tone with journalists when asked about ammunition shortages and US casualties.

Hegseth is a member of the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches, founded in 1998 by evangelical pastor Douglas Wilson, who has used Islamophobic rhetoric while discussing Muslim immigrants to the US.

item.description:
UN General Assembly 2026: US-Israeli war on Iran to take centre stage

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 09/21/2026 - 18:36
Trump, Iran’s president and other leaders will address the assembly as diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict remain stalled
People walk past the United Nations Headquarters in New York City, on 21 September 2026 (David 'Dee' Delgado/Reuters)
Off

World leaders will converge on New York City this week for a United Nations General Assembly overshadowed by the US and Israeli war on Iran.

US President Donald Trump is scheduled to address the assembly early on Tuesday, returning to the UN a year after claiming US strikes had dealt a decisive blow to Iran's nuclear programme.

This time, however, he faces a sceptical international audience as Iran challenges Washington by restricting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, threatening a vital artery for global energy supplies and raising fears of further disruption to the world economy.

The pressure is also mounting beyond the Gulf.

Days before the UN gathering, Yemen's Houthis rapidly expanded their control along the Red Sea coast, capturing territory overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another strategic chokepoint through which a significant share of global trade passes.

The US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told reporters on Friday that Trump would focus his speech on his administration's handling of international conflicts and the threat posed by Iran's nuclear programme.

"The president will highlight how he has and his administration have confronted complex problems head-on around the world," Waltz said.

"He will touch on the importance of ensuring that Iran never has a nuclear weapon.”

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to address the General Assembly on Wednesday, accompanied by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

His appearance will give Tehran a platform to set out its position on the war and challenge Washington's account of the conflict before the same international audience addressed by Trump a day earlier.

The week-long meeting, however, comes as the UN struggles to remain relevant, with many state leaders opting to skip the event entirely.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, who last participated in the UN gathering remotely in 2021, will not travel to New York City. Instead, he is expected to hold bilateral talks with Trump in Washington on Thursday.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has not attended the event for more than a decade, will be sending Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

The leaders of India, Germany and South Africa are also reportedly sending their representatives.

Gaza and occupied Palestine

The war in Gaza is expected to feature prominently during the summit. 

Erdogan and Burnham to meet for first time at UN General Assembly in New York
Read More »

Despite being the subject of an arrest warrant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Thursday.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, however, will not be able to attend the gathering in person for a second consecutive year after the US extended its ban on Palestinian officials.

The Trump administration said the denial of entry was due to Palestinian actions to "internationalise the Israeli-Palestinian conflict", including pursuing cases against Israel at international tribunals.

The General Assembly voted on Thursday to allow Abbas to participate by video.

Diplomats said a high-level meeting is also expected to take place alongside the General Assembly to advance efforts towards a two-state solution for Israelis and Palestinians, although significant progress is not expected.

Sudan and the wider Middle East  

Diplomats also expect a high-level meeting on Sudan's war to take place on the sidelines of the assembly.

Sudan has been engulfed in war since April 2023, when a power struggle between the country's military and the Rapid Support Forces erupted into conflict.

The fighting has forced more than 14 million people from their homes and triggered one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises.

Sudanese army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, who became the country's de facto head of state following the 2019 ousting of longtime President Omar al-Bashir, is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Thursday.

Trump will also meet with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi at some point during the UN gathering, Iraqi outlets have reported.

A Turkish Airlines aircraft lands at the Damascus International Airport in the Syrian capital, on 23 January 2025 (Bakr Alkasem/AFP)
Off

Turkey's national carrier, Turkish Airlines, and budget airlines AJet and Pegasus have cancelled flights to and from Iran from 21 September as US sanctions take effect, a review by Middle East Eye indicates.

The Turkish Airlines and AJet websites have no flights to Iran until March, while Pegasus appears to have removed all flights to the country from its booking system for the foreseeable future.

Iran International reported that a Turkish Airlines representative told the channel there was no guarantee flights would resume even after March 2027.

A person familiar with the issue told MEE that US Treasury sanctions on Iran's aviation sector were so severe that Turkish carriers had been forced to suspend their flights.

The person said that while restrictions on US-manufactured aircraft, such as Boeing planes, were understandable, the new sanctions also prevented Airbus aircraft from flying to Iran because they contained American-made components.

The carriers had no other choice, the person added.

A Turkish official said that as of Monday, Mahan Air was the only Iranian carrier barred from flying to Turkey, leaving other Iranian airlines free to maintain services between the two countries for now.

Turkey and Iran have maintained a stable relationship and extensive energy and commercial ties despite successive rounds of US sanctions on Tehran. However, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has taken a different approach since US President Donald Trump moved to tighten economic pressure on Iran.

Over the weekend, Turkey revoked the banking licence of Iran's Bank Mellat, which had operated in the country for decades.

Turkey's banking regulator also took over Golden Global Investment Bank last week after the US imposed sanctions on the institution for allegedly transferring funds to the Iranian government.

Jason Eaton faces up to life in prison after a jury rejected that he was suffering from delusions
This undated handout photo provided by the Institute for Middle East Understanding shows Hisham Awartani, Tahseen Ali, and Kenan Abdulhamid, who were wounded on 25 November 2023 (AFP)
Off

The man charged with shooting three young Palestinian college students in 2023 in the US state of Vermont was found guilty of three counts of attempted second-degree murder on Monday.

The victims, Hisham Awartani, Kinnan Abdel Hamid and Tahseen Ahmed, were on their way to a family dinner when they were shot by 51-year-old Jason Eaton. They were speaking in Arabic, and two of them were wearing keffiyehs.

Lawyers for Eaton had argued that he was suffering from delusions during the shootings, saying that he believed voices, which he thought were from CIA agents, told him to carry out the attack to protect a Jewish family in his neighbourhood.

The attack left Awartani, who was a student at Brown University at the time, paralysed from the chest down.

“The verdict cannot undo what happened or erase the trauma our families still carry, but it affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did,” Awartani’s mother, Elizabeth Price, told reporters after the decision.

The families, however, criticised the decision not to categorise the attack as a hate crime. In Vermont, recent hate crime charges have been filed only when a defendant explicitly uttered a slur during the crime.

“This was a hate crime. We have said so from the beginning. The law never made him answer for it. But we know what he did," the families said in a statement after the verdict.

The three victims were wearing their keffiyehs in the courtroom, while the judge ordered other observers to remove their keffiyehs due to “concern about how that would impact the jury", according to the New York Times.
